articles.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
articles.text:
DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  Texas A&M University
- Summary:
  Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.
- Share:
How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.
Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.
Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists
One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.
This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.
Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.
To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.
DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage
The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.
"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," said Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule."
This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.
The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.
New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection
Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.
The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.
"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.
These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.
Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?
With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.
A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.
"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins."
By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Texas A&M University. Original written by Amy Leifeste. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Keyvan Khosh Abady, Negar Karpourazar, Peter M. Rentzepis. UV photodamage pathways and the evolutionary selection of thymine over uracil in early genetic systems. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (33) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2615278123

articles.title: Ancient ‘supermountains’ under Antarctica supercharged complex life on Earth, study claims
articles.text:
Ancient 'supermountains' under Antarctica supercharged complex life on Earth, study claims — but not everyone agrees
A study claims that ancient 'supervolcanoes' hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.
Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica. They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions.
About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive.
Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia.
"The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko, a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.
"The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica."
Ancient minerals
Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet, so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history.
To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science.
They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales.
"We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said.
Alan Collins, an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email.
The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found.
Elias Rugen, a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said.
However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said.
Sedimentary life source
The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said.
"In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean."
Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit.
In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth.
Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion. The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans).
The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web.
However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing."
Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship."
However, the study did show that there was much more to discover under the ice in Antarctica.
"The most exciting aspect is the possibility that some of the largest mountain systems in Earth's history are effectively hidden beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet," Daczko said. "Antarctica potentially holds some of the most important remaining evidence for understanding the tectonic and environmental evolution of our planet."
How much do you know about Earth's frozen continent? Test your smarts with our Antarctica quiz!
Sarah Wild is a British-South African freelance science journalist. She has written about particle physics, cosmology and everything in between. She studied physics, electronics and English literature at Rhodes University, South Africa, and later read for an MSc Medicine in bioethics.
Since she started perpetrating journalism for a living, she's written books, won awards, and run national science desks. Her work has appeared in Nature, Science, Scientific American, and The Observer, among others. In 2017 she won a gold AAAS Kavli for her reporting on forensics in South Africa.

articles.title: Satellites watch volcanic eruptions add new beaches on Iwo Jima
articles.text:
Satellites watch volcanic eruptions add new beaches on Iwo Jima | Space photo of the day for Nov. 25, 2026
The island is growing, but will it last?
Iwo Jima looks remarkably different from space after a volcanic eruption created new land extending the Japanese island's beaches.
What is it?
On Oct. 27, Japan's Meteorological Agency detected an underwater volcanic eruption off the shores of Iwo Jima. Soon after this initial detection of the "submarine" volcano, satellites orbiting our planet started taking a look, observing to see what havoc this eruption might wreak.
When you compare the satellite images above captured by the Landsat 9 satellite's Operational Land Imager (OLI), you can see the stark differences between the island on October 26 before the eruption and weeks later on November 11.
The island was also observed by NASA's NISAR spacecraft as well as the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors. Together, this imagery gave researchers a more complete picture of how the eruption continued and the effects it left behind.
And amazingly, with satellite imagery experts have been able to show that the eruption has actually added more land to the island's beaches.
Why is it incredible?
On Nov. 16, Japan's Coast Guard confirmed in a statement that about 125 acres (50 hectares) of new land is now connected to the island's southeast beach following the recent volcanic eruption.
This is not the first time that a volcano has created new land. Lava and ash from a volcanic eruption can solidify and accumulate, adding land material around the volcano or to a nearby coast if it is located offshore or underwater, as we saw in this case.
But these new landforms aren't always permanent fixtures. This new addition to the island's beach could easily and quickly be washed away by the waves, which happened on Iwo Jima just a few years ago in 2023. And experts expect the same thing to happen with this new land.
"I imagine we'll see this new land wash away within a few months," Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center who has previously studied landforms created by volcanic eruptions, said in a statement. "But we'll have to wait and see."

articles.title: AI-designed protein tricks defective insulin receptors into working in new mouse study
articles.text:
'Like designing a new key to open a defective lock': AI-designed protein tricks defective insulin receptors into working
Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.
A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't.
The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance, in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone.
In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine, researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition.
When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down.
But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance. In one of the most severe forms, called Donohue syndrome, children can experience dangerously high blood sugar after eating, and unusually low blood sugar between meals, as well as poor growth. Most children with the condition die before their first birthday.
"Some [of these] patients produce extremely high levels of insulin, but their receptors cannot respond properly," study co-author Eunhee Choi, a cell biologist at Columbia University, told Live Science. "Simply giving more insulin may not solve the problem."
That's why Choi and her colleagues explored whether they could activate the receptor in another way.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
In 2025, the researchers used computational tools, including AlphaFold2, an AI program that predicts protein structures and how they fit together, to develop proteins that activate insulin receptors in a different way than insulin does. In that previous study, one of those proteins, RF-409, lowered blood sugar in both healthy mice and mice with obesity. In the new research, the team wanted to see whether RF-409 could also activate defective insulin receptors.
First, they ran experiments with laboratory-grown mouse and rat cells and with healthy mice, both with working insulin receptors. This confirmed that RF-409 largely mimicked insulin's effects on cellular signaling and metabolism. In the mice, RF-409 had a nearly 60-fold longer half-life in the bloodstream than insulin, meaning the protein stays in circulation much longer before breaking down.
"Both these features make [the finding] more than just an elegant trick," said Dr. Rajiv Agarwal, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Unlike a protein that mimics only some of insulin's effects, RF-409 reproduces most of its normal signaling, "which matters in children who need growth as well as glucose control," he added.
To test how RF-409 works with defective receptors, the researchers focused on a mutation previously identified in patients with Donohue syndrome; this genetic mutation alters a key part of the receptor's structure, preventing insulin from binding to it. Computer models suggested that RF-409 could bypass the affected region and hold the receptor in the shape needed to transmit signals inside cells.
The researchers genetically engineered mice to carry this mutation. Compared with mice that retained a functioning copy of the insulin receptor gene, these mice had, on average, roughly 2.5 times higher blood sugar and 10 times higher fasting insulin levels (the amount of insulin in blood after a period without food).
When injected with insulin, mice with defective receptors showed no substantial drop in blood sugar. Treatment with RF-409, however, lowered mice's blood sugar by roughly 60% within two hours.
"It is like designing a new key to open a defective lock," said Kalaiarasan Ponnusamy, a computational biologist at SRM Institute of Science and Technology in India who was not involved in the study. "From a computational protein-design perspective, this is a major advance because it demonstrates that entirely new proteins can be engineered to restore receptor function without correcting the underlying genetic mutation."
After 14 days of continuous treatment, five mice given RF-409 had lower blood sugar, maintained their body weight and retained more abdominal fat than five mice given a saline solution, for comparison. The treated mice also showed less pancreatic damage.
"Extending this approach to other disease-causing receptor mutations is a realistic possibility, provided the receptor retains its ability to transmit signals," Ponnusamy said. Some mutations, for instance, prevent insulin receptors from reaching the cell surface or transmitting signals inside cells at all. That means the technique demonstrated in the study is unlikely to work against such mutations.
Identifying which mutations can be treated in this way is now a priority for Choi. The team also plans to investigate how RF-409 affects different tissues in the body and whether it remains safe and effective over longer periods of treatment, she said.
Although Agarwal foresees several hurdles in bringing RF-409 into clinical use; for instance, the immune system's reaction to the protein will have to be carefully studied, and in general, it's challenging to run trials with infants with rare disorders. That said, he remains hopeful that it could help patients whose diseases have no treatments to treat the underlying cause.
"This is the first approach I have seen that addresses the actual defect rather than working around it," he said.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Hung, A., Wang, X., Gao, M., Ng, M., Oliinyk, D., Weaver, R., Zollbrecht, E., Cardoso, S., Ronel, G. S., Paolucci, C., Ye, J., Fan, Q. R., Rhea, E., Mann, M., Baker, D., Accili, D., & Choi, E. (2026). Reprogramming insulin receptor activation with a de novo agonist to overcome severe preclinical insulin resistance. Science Translational Medicine, 18, eaei0487. https://dx.doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.aei0487

He regularly writes for The Hindu and has contributed to The Wire Science, where he conveys complex biomedical research to the public in accessible language. articles.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
articles.text:
A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  University of Cambridge
- Summary:
  At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
- Share:
At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.
The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.
In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.
Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.
A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation
One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.
To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.
They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.
The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.
This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.
"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.
He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject."
Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.
Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?
The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.
By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.
"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.
He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine."
Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.
Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island
Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.
He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.
The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.
Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

Journal Reference:

Robeck, Steve Horvath, Christopher Faulk, Yanjun Ma, Stephen W. Clark. Epigenetic insights into extreme longevity in the world’s oldest terrestrial animal, Jonathan. articles.title: Watch live: Europe unveils 1st close-up views of asteroid Dimorphos after NASA's DART impact
articles.text:
Watch live: Europe unveils 1st close-up views of asteroid Dimorphos after NASA's DART impact
Hera is arriving to surveil the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission that slammed a kinetic impactor into a double asteroid system four years ago.
After a two-year journey, the Hera spacecraft is arriving at the Didymos double asteroid system, and its first images are being released to the public today (Nov. 25).
The European Space Agency's (ESA's ) Hera probe launched atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 7, 2024. Its destination is the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos, a "rubble pile" asteroid, and its smaller moonlet Dimorphos. NASA slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in 2022 in the historic DART test, which confirmed that such an impact can alter the trajectory of an asteroid.
Hera arrives at Didymos today, and ESA is sharing the first close-up images from the mission in a free online livestream. ESA's livestream starts at 1:45 p.m. ET (1845 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 25). Watch it live here, courtesy of the European Space Agency.
At Dimorphos, Hera will inspect the wreckage caused by DART (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), humanity's first test of planetary defense. The test was designed to see if the orbit of a threatening asteroid could be altered, taking it off a potential crash course with Earth.
The DART mission succeeded, shortening Dimorphos' orbit by just over 30 minutes, showing that kinetic impacts can indeed alter the trajectories of asteroids.
Hera will now show up to the crash scene and study the impact crater left by DART and inspect any changes the collision caused. Scientists are thrilled by the prospects.
"ESA's Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know," the mission's principal investigator Patrick Michel said in an ESA statement. "How did the impact change Dimorphos? What is the mass of the asteroid and which of its properties explain its response to DART impact?
"Hera is carrying out a thorough investigation ever of a deflected asteroid, packed with scientific firsts, to give us a complete and unbiased picture of humankind's first planetary defense test."
ESA has already shared some of the remarkable images Hera has captured en route to Didymos, including a breathtaking image of both asteroids as Dimorphos cast its shadow on its larger companion in a deep-space double-asteroid solar eclipse.
Hera even stopped by Mars on its way to the asteroids, snapping pictures of its moon Deimos.
Hera will remain at the Didymos-Dimorphos system for months, deploying cubesats that will study the asteroids with visible and infrared light cameras and radar instruments.
Through Hera, scientists hope to refine planetary defense techniques so that, should the time ever come, humanity has options for defending itself against incoming space rocks like the one that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
"Through many years of hard work our international collaboration managed to do just that, and for the very highest of intentions: to help make Earth safer," said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli.
Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

articles.title: California braces for triple flooding threat as 'king tides' overlap with 'super' El Niño
articles.text:
California braces for triple flooding threat as 'king tides' overlap with 'super' El Niño
Exceptionally high tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and abnormally warm water are converging on California's coast, with authorities urging residents to limit unnecessary travel this Thanksgiving.
Major flooding of up to 2.7 feet (0.8 meters) is expected in parts of California today (Nov. 25) as record-breaking tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and warmer-than-average ocean water converge along the state's coast.
The triple flooding threat is expected to hit the San Francisco Bay Area especially hard, with San Francisco International Airport and other low-lying areas of the city bracing for deluges, while officials warned of dangerous breaking waves measuring 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) tall along San Francisco's coast, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Meanwhile, in Southern California, coastal communities should expect potentially record-breaking "king tides" and breaking waves up to 15 feet (4.6 m) high, the National Weather Service warned on its website. King tides are exceptionally high tides that occur every year due to seasonal factors and the alignment of Earth, the sun and the moon — but this year's "super" El Niño has amplified the risk by pushing a massive "Kelvin wave" up California's coast.
Citing the forecast, several cities on California's central coast have closed beaches to shield people from hazards, including sudden waves that could wash beachgoers out to sea. Local authorities have also urged residents to limit unnecessary travel during the Thanksgiving holiday.
"As Californians head into the holiday, take a few minutes to check travel conditions, sign up for local emergency alerts, and make a plan to keep your family safe," California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday (Nov. 24).
The flooding comes as a perfect storm of adverse conditions has gathered on California's coastline. Scientists expected the king tides and the coastal flooding associated with them to emerge this time of the year. However, these powerful tides are now arriving on top of blistering sea temperatures due to accelerating climate change and the current El Niño event — the warm phase of a multiyear natural climate pattern that's in full swing and set to intensify through the end of the year.
Ocean water expands as it warms, swelling tides and raising the risk of strong surf and big waves. As a result, this year's tides are predicted to be at their highest levels since January 1983, when tides also coincided with El Niño-fueled storms, AFP reported.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
- 'This is such a clear story': Climate change is supercharging El Niño to unprecedented strengths, study finds
- The super El Niño could cause torrential rainstorms. Americans may need to stock up on food to prepare, experts say.
- Super El Niño may push an already stressed climate ecosystem across a critical threshold, climate change researcher says
In January 1983, "all hell broke loose," Reinhard Flick, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, told AFP. "We had 13-foot (4-meter) waves offshore, the highest tides of the year, and hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It hit Northern California, Southern California, everybody."
Forecasts suggest this week's conditions won't be quite that bad. But there are risks to be aware of going into winter, especially as El Niño has yet to peak and more king tides are expected in December and January.
"It could potentially be quite bad if we also have rainfall and high waves at the same time during any one of these big events, especially December and January, when rainfall generally increases on our coast," Flick said.
Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
articles.text:
Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
- Date:
  November 22, 2026
- Source:
  University of Pennsylvania School of Medicine
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.
- Share:
A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.
An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.
Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.
A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago
The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered new genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.
The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.
The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.
At first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.
"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first."
How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision
The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.
Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.
Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.
One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.
However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.
"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost."
The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.
What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss
An important question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?
Researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.
Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.
"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems."
By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.
The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

- Chloe M. Stanton, Georg Ansari, Kristina Pfau, Theresa Lipsky, Mihail Halachev, Lukas Gerasimavicius, Camilla Drake, Joseph A. articles.title: Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe
articles.text:
Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe
The supermassive black hole, known as Dún Aonghasa, is unlike any other seen at a similar period of the early universe.
The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.
The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar.
The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.
Quasars occur when supermassive black holes are surrounded by vast amounts of gas and dust on which they feed. The immense gravitational influence of the black hole causes this material, in the form of an accretion disk, to glow brightly and to blast out bright jets of plasma. That means quasars at the heart of galaxies in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs) like this one can often be brighter than the combined light of every star in the entire surrounding galaxy, but only briefly.
The newly discovered quasar, designated J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, is in this brief phase of its existence. It was discovered among millions of objects in 18 months of data from Euclid.
Euclid's initial observation of Dún Aonghasa was followed up by an array of ground-based and space-based telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). It was the JWST that determined the mass of this supermassive black hole.
What is interesting about Dún Aonghasa is that it is unlike other supermassive black holes seen at a similar period of the early universe. That's because this black hole is feeding relatively slowly. That means if it engaged in rapid feeding to reach its massive size, that period of gorging on gas and dust has either ended or it has paused.
That is something that further complicates our picture of supermassive black hole growth.
By staring back 13.1 billion years in time to see Dún Aonghasa, Euclid is also observing a crucial time in cosmic history when the first stars and galaxies were taking shape, and the clearing of cosmic gas was ending the dark ages of our universe by allowing light to travel freely.
Euclid's primary mission is improving our understanding of dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe, and dark matter, the most mysterious "stuff" in the cosmos. Collectively, these aspects of the universe account for around 95% of its matter-energy budget and have come to be collectively referred to as the dark universe. Hence Euclid's nickname as the "dark universe detective."
This research, along with Euclid's discovery of at least 12 that date back around 13 billion years, shows that this pioneering space telescope launched in 2023 could also make a major contribution to our understanding of black holes and their growth.
The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

articles.title: 100,000-year-old tooth found in Chinese cave may be from unknown human lineage
articles.text:
Scientists may have discovered new branch on the human family tree, 100,000-year-old tooth in China suggests
One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.
In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage.
In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature, researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo" group, the researchers wrote.
The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating, the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old.
To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different.
The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus, but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens, including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown.
The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor, an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans.
The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
A new branch?
Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution, researchers say.
Denisovans were first identified in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes, a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins.
The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor, two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus.
It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.
"We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins."
"There is more to learn"
The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo'. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email.
Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus, then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave.
"I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers" that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses."
The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate.
"We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said.
Xing, S., Rao, H., Xie, G., Bai, F., Ge, J., Bennett, E.A., Wu, Z., Shao, Q., Li, X., Viola, B., Sun, Q., Zhou, K., Li, Z., Jiangzuo, Q., Zhao, Y., Liu, F., Liu, Y., Feng, X., Lin, Q., Fu, Q. (2026). Middle-Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China. Nature. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11341-6
Human evolution quiz: What do you know about Homo sapiens?
Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

Journal Reference:

articles.title: November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)
articles.text:
November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)
From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.
The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.
Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.
November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.
That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.
Best photos of the November 2026 full Beaver Moon
Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.
Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.
Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of New York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.
NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.
Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.
This shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.
Our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.
"Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up."
This striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.
Allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.
"Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image."
Moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?
Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.
That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.
Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

The final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

articles.title: A woman gulped ice-cold drinks and ended up with torn arteries — Diagnostic dilemma
articles.text:
A woman gulped ice-cold drinks and ended up with torn arteries — Diagnostic dilemma
A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.
The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California
The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes.
About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out.
What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department.
An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department.
There, a third blood test showed that her troponin level had risen even further, and doctors diagnosed a heart attack. An angiogram — a scan that shows the structure of blood vessels — revealed a small tear in a branch of her right coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart.
About 30 hours after she was discharged, the woman developed similar chest pain after taking several gulps of ice-cold green tea and subsequently jogging up a flight of stairs. The pain began when she reached the top of the stairs and was accompanied by the same lightheaded feeling she had experienced before.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
She called 911 and was again brought to an emergency department, and although an initial EKG showed no clear signs of a heart attack, subsequent recordings revealed heart-activity changes consistent with one. A second angiogram revealed a new tear in the left circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery.
The diagnosis: Doctors diagnosed the woman with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), a condition in which a tear develops in the wall of a coronary artery. In SCAD, blood collects within the artery wall, and this compresses the channel that blood normally flows through to reach the heart. As in the patient's case, this compression can sometimes trigger heart attacks by drastically restricting the heart's blood supply.
Doctors also found fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) in a blood vessel in the woman's pelvis. FMD changes the structure of artery walls, making them too weak or too stiff, and it's known to occur in some people with SCAD. It may have made her arteries more prone to tearing, the doctors wrote in a report of the case.
The treatment: During her first emergency department visit, doctors gave the woman aspirin, fluids, medicine for nausea and an antacid. Her chest pain eventually went away. At the second visit, doctors gave her the blood thinner heparin to reduce blood clotting and the beta-blocker metoprolol to slow her heart rate. She was discharged the following morning with prescriptions for cholesterol- and blood-pressure-lowering drugs.
After the second episode, doctors gave her opioid painkillers and medicine for nausea to take as needed, along with aspirin and a cholesterol-lowering drug. The cholesterol-lowering drug was soon stopped because she did not have high cholesterol. Doctors eventually stopped the blood-pressure medication, too, after a follow-up heart ultrasound showed that the affected part of her heart was moving normally again.
She continued taking nebivolol, a different beta-blocker that slows the heart rate and can reduce stress on the organ, for years after these two episodes. And for several months after the second episode, the woman avoided cold drinks on her own initiative. She gradually reintroduced them, taking small sips rather than gulping. Ten years later, she remained free of symptoms, the report noted.
What makes this case unique: Years later, the woman learned that cold drinks had been linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. She told her healthcare team that she suspected cold drinks might have triggered SCAD in her case, too.
Separately, a 2017 case report described another woman who developed chest pain and a heart attack after drinking cold water. Doctors subsequently found that she had SCAD and FMD. However, that report did not investigate cold water as a possible trigger of the patient's symptoms.
The authors of the current report proposed that rapidly swallowing a cold drink may trigger a brief rise in blood pressure, known as a pressor response. This is associated with increased activation of the body's fight-or-flight system, which can then release stress hormones. These changes may make the heart contract more forcefully and cause the coronary arteries to narrow temporarily, thereby increasing the forces acting on their walls. In someone whose arteries are susceptible to tears, that added stress could contribute to rips in the tissue and the accumulation of blood within the artery wall.
However, the report authors stressed that they cannot establish that cold drinks caused the woman's dissections in this instance. They hope their findings will encourage doctors to ask patients with SCAD about potential triggers, but they said further research is needed to determine whether rapidly drinking cold beverages can really trigger the condition.
For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Heringer, G. V., Smith, C. M., Takeuchi, K., Goh, C. H., & Vinson, D. R. (2026). Association of ice-cold drink ingestion with spontaneous coronary artery dissection: a case report. BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12872-026-06669-w

Anirban Mukhopadhyay is an independent science journalist. He holds a PhD in genetics and a master’s in computational biology and drug design. He regularly writes for The Hindu and has contributed to The Wire Science, where he conveys complex biomedical research to the public in accessible language. Beyond science writing, he enjoys creating and reading fiction that blends myth, memory, and melancholy into surreal tales exploring grief, identity, and the quiet magic of self-discovery. In his free time, he loves long walks with his dog and motorcycling across The Himalayas.
